prompt_c2:
You are a streetscape inventory annotator. Look ONLY at the uploaded streetscape image.
Return JSON ONLY. No markdown, no commentary, no reasoning.
 Task: record what is visible in the scene. Do not score, do not give design advice.
 Schema:
{
"road_type": "highway|arterial|neighborhood_street|alley|plaza|unclear",
"elements": {
"sidewalk": "true|false|unclear",
"bike_lane": "true|false|unclear",
"seating": "true|false|unclear",
"shade_trees": "none|few|many|unclear",
"curb_ramp": "true|false|unclear",
"tactile_paving": "true|false|unclear",
"pedestrian_crossing": "true|false|unclear",
"street_lighting": "true|false|unclear",
"greenery": "none|low|medium|high|unclear",
"vehicle_traffic": "none|light|heavy|unclear",
"bus_stop": "true|false|unclear"
},
"issues": ["no_seating", "little_shade", "no_bike_lane", "poor_accessibility", "narrow_sidewalk", "no_crossing", "high_traffic_exposure"],
"brief": "One or two English sentences describing the visible street scene."
}
 Rules:
- If an element is not clearly visible, use "unclear". Do not guess.
- "issues" may only list problems that are visible. Use [] if none.
- "brief" must mention concrete objects (sidewalk, trees, lanes, benches, ramps, etc.).

Living-service roads The activity groups on living-service roads include residents and workers around the road, as well as people from other areas who come for shopping and strolling. The paving surface layer shall use natural, aesthetically pleasing, comfortable, and ecological materials, while also meeting the requirement of coordination with the surrounding landscape. 12 Figure 1.4-4 Example of paving for scenic leisure roads D. Historic-style streets and lanes The paving design of historic-style streets and lanes shall continue and reflect cultural charm and local character, and shape distinctive spaces. Road design should focus on creating a historical and cultural atmosphere. The paving materials and texture shall be integrated with the surrounding environment. Figure 1.4-5 Example of paving for historic-style streets and lanes E. Comprehensive roads Comprehensive roads have a relatively high degree of mixing in road functions and interface types. They shall take into account the different needs of multiple characteristics, optimize the slow-traffic travel experience, consider the composite needs of road functions and the businesses on both sides, and create a paving system that is highly adaptable and simple and elegant. Article 46 Local people’s governments at or above the county level shall organize relevant departments to study and analyze the causes of road traffic congestion, formulate road traffic congestion governance plans, and implement road traffic congestion governance measures. The traffic management department of the public security organ shall promptly release road conditions information and road traffic congestion warnings, guide traffic travel, and alleviate road traffic congestion. Except for temporary measures implemented due to emergencies, measures such as restricting or prohibiting passage shall be announced to the public five working days in advance; where they have a major impact on the public, opinions of the public shall be solicited in advance and made public. In road sections and places prone to road traffic congestion, the relevant operating and management units shall assist the traffic management department of the public security organ in directing vehicles and pedestrians. Chapter V Rules for Road Passage Article 47 The following vehicles and devices shall not be allowed to travel on roads: (1) Non-road vehicles such as forklifts, sightseeing vehicles in enclosed areas, scooters, unicycles, and balance vehicles; (2) Sliding devices such as skateboards and roller skates; (3) Other vehicles, devices, and the like that are prohibited from traveling on roads by laws and regulations. Article 48 Vehicles and pedestrians shall each use their respective lanes. On roads without separate motor vehicle lanes, non-motor vehicle lanes, or sidewalks, motor vehicles shall travel in the middle of the road, non-motor vehicles shall travel along the right side of the road, and pedestrians shall travel on both sides of the road. When non-motor vehicles overtake non-motor vehicles or pedestrians ahead on the road, they shall do so only after confirming that there is sufficient safety distance. Article 49 Vehicles entering or leaving roads shall yield priority passage to vehicles and pedestrians normally traveling on the road. Motor vehicles entering or leaving non-motor vehicle lanes or sidewalks shall not impede the normal passage of non-motor vehicles or pedestrians. Vehicles entering or leaving parking lots (garages) or road parking spaces shall not impede the normal passage of other vehicles or pedestrians. Article 50 Vehicles using another lane for passage or changing lanes shall comply with the following provisions: (1) Yield priority passage to vehicles and pedestrians traveling in the lane being used; (2) Not impede the normal passage of other vehicles or pedestrians; (3) Travel in sequence and order, not change lanes frequently, and not continuously change more than two motor vehicle lanes at one time; (4) When vehicles in the left and right lanes both change into the same lane, vehicles in the left lane shall yield to vehicles in the right lane; (5) Other provisions of laws and regulations concerning vehicles using another lane for passage or changing

passages.text: and acceptance criteria shall be formulated in accordance with design requirements and site conditions. 1.1.5 Maintenance Key Points 1. Sidewalks shall be firm and level, with no cracks, missing bricks, damage, or other defects; joint widths shall be uniform and joints fully filled. All manhole covers shall be flush with the sidewalk elevation and in good condition, and their strength must meet sidewalk traffic requirements. 2. Sidewalks must have a base course and bedding course of sufficient strength. For settlement, breakage, or damage caused by insufficient base-course strength, the base course shall first be reinforced before the surface blocks are repaved. 3. To ensure safe pedestrian passage in rain and snow, the longitudinal slope of sidewalk ramps shall be ≤1:20. Smooth-surfaced ramp slabs shall be treated with anti-slip measures. Ramps that do not meet the requirements shall be demolished and reconstructed during rectification. 1.2 At-Grade Crossing System 1.2.1 Crossing at At-Grade Intersections 1. Basic Principles A. The slow-traffic organization for pedestrians and non-motor vehicles within grade-separated interchange areas shall be continuous, safe, and convenient, and should be arranged at ground level to avoid pedestrians and non-motor vehicles having to go up and down or increasing detour distances. 2. Quality Enhancement A. Reducing crossing distance Reducing the curb radius at intersections can effectively lower turning speeds, shorten pedestrian crossing distances, and enlarge pedestrian waiting areas. The facility strip or green belt along the roadside may also be appropriately used to create a pedestrian stopping space. Table 1.2-1 Recommended Curb Radius Values | Road class | Recommended curb radius (m) | |---|---:| | Main and secondary arterial roads | 5–10 | | Branch roads | 5–8 | Note: For exclusive right-turn lanes with traffic islands, the recommended curb radius is 8–10 m. Figure 1.2-1 Reducing Road Curb Radius B. Secondary crossing refuge island When the pedestrian or bicycle crossing traverses more than 4 lanes of two-way motor vehicle traffic, or when the crossing length exceeds 16 m, a secondary crossing refuge island shall be set in the center of the road. The island width shall not be less than 2 m, and in difficult circumstances not less than 1.5 m. On roads with a median strip (or where lane width can be reduced), pedestrian crossings on signal-free sections shall be provided with a “Z”-shaped secondary crossing refuge island. The refuge island length shall not be less than 8 m, and corresponding guardrails shall be installed. Figure 1.2-2 Schematic Diagram of a “Z”-Shaped Secondary Crossing Refuge Island I C. All-direction cross intersection For intersections surrounded by relatively dense commercial facilities and heavy pedestrian flows, an “all-direction cross intersection” may be used as appropriate. This not only improves pedestrian crossing efficiency, but also prevents interference between pedestrians and motor vehicles. D. Improving the experience of non-motor vehicle crossings Intersections with large non-motor vehicle crossing volumes should be equipped with dedicated non-motor vehicle signal lights. At branch-road intersections with heavy non-motor vehicle traffic, explore moving the non-motor vehicle crossing waiting area in front of the motor vehicle stop line and granting an early green signal priority.  1. Evaluation Dimensions
Justice: Analyze whether the environment fairly distributes spatial resources, including Equity (rationality of asset distribution), Fairness (non-discriminatory rules), and Accessibility (barrier-free physical design).
Comfort: Analyze physical perception at a micro-scale, including Thermal Comfort (shade/vegetation), Physical Comfort (paving/seating), and Psychological Comfort (noise/crowding).
Core Indicators: Safety, Livability, Sustainability, Aesthetics, Walkability, and Bikeability.
 2. Persona Perspective Requirements:
The analysis must strictly adhere to the persona's characteristics. For example:
Persons with Disabilities: Focus on curb ramps, continuity of tactile paving (blind tracks), and physical obstacles.
Elderly: Focus on resting facilities, slope gradients, and summer shade.
Teenagers: Focus on traffic calming measures and social surveillance (Eyes on the street).
 3. How to use the image vs retrieved knowledge:
- The IMAGE is the primary evidence. Score only what is visible or reasonably inferable from the photo.
- Section 6 provides retrieved guidelines and research. Use them to interpret the image (what the scene should provide for this persona/indicators), not to invent objects that are not in the photo.
- If retrieved text conflicts with the image, trust the image and say so in the explanation.
- Explanations must cite specific visible objects (benches, ramps, tree shade, lane markings, etc.). When a guideline is used, briefly connect it to those objects.

Scenic leisure roads According to the characteristics of scenic leisure roads and the behavioral characteristics of the activity groups, the design objective of the paved area is to provide a safe, comfortable slow-traffic environment and leisure space. Historic-style streets and lanes The paving design of historic-style streets and lanes shall continue and reflect cultural charm and local character, and shape distinctive spaces. Road design should focus on creating a historical and cultural atmosphere. The paving materials and texture shall be integrated with the surrounding environment. Article 46 Local people’s governments at or above the county level shall organize relevant departments to study and analyze the causes of road traffic congestion, formulate road traffic congestion governance plans, and implement road traffic congestion governance measures. The traffic management department of the public security organ shall promptly release road conditions information and road traffic congestion warnings, guide traffic travel, and alleviate road traffic congestion. Except for temporary measures implemented due to emergencies, measures such as restricting or prohibiting passage shall be announced to the public five working days in advance; where they have a major impact on the public, opinions of the public shall be solicited in advance and made public. In road sections and places prone to road traffic congestion, the relevant operating and management units shall assist the traffic management department of the public security organ in directing vehicles and pedestrians. Chapter V Rules for Road Passage Article 47 The following vehicles and devices shall not be allowed to travel on roads: (1) Non-road vehicles such as forklifts, sightseeing vehicles in enclosed areas, scooters, unicycles, and balance vehicles; (2) Sliding devices such as skateboards and roller skates; (3) Other vehicles, devices, and the like that are prohibited from traveling on roads by laws and regulations. Article 48 Vehicles and pedestrians shall each use their respective lanes. On roads without separate motor vehicle lanes, non-motor vehicle lanes, or sidewalks, motor vehicles shall travel in the middle of the road, non-motor vehicles shall travel along the right side of the road, and pedestrians shall travel on both sides of the road. When non-motor vehicles overtake non-motor vehicles or pedestrians ahead on the road, they shall do so only after confirming that there is sufficient safety distance. Article 49 Vehicles entering or leaving roads shall yield priority passage to vehicles and pedestrians normally traveling on the road. Motor vehicles entering or leaving non-motor vehicle lanes or sidewalks shall not impede the normal passage of non-motor vehicles or pedestrians. Vehicles entering or leaving parking lots (garages) or road parking spaces shall not impede the normal passage of other vehicles or pedestrians. Article 50 Vehicles using another lane for passage or changing lanes shall comply with the following provisions: (1) Yield priority passage to vehicles and pedestrians traveling in the lane being used; (2) Not impede the normal passage of other vehicles or pedestrians; (3) Travel in sequence and order, not change lanes frequently, and not continuously change more than two motor vehicle lanes at one time; (4) When vehicles in the left and right lanes both change into the same lane, vehicles in the left lane shall yield to vehicles in the right lane; (5) Other provisions of laws and regulations concerning vehicles using another lane for passage or changing

Sidewalks shall be firm and level, with no cracks, missing bricks, damage, or other defects; joint widths shall be uniform and joints fully filled. All manhole covers shall be flush with the sidewalk elevation and in good condition, and their strength must meet sidewalk traffic requirements. 2. Sidewalks must have a base course and bedding course of sufficient strength. To ensure safe pedestrian passage in rain and snow, the longitudinal slope of sidewalk ramps shall be ≤1:20. Smooth-surfaced ramp slabs shall be treated with anti-slip measures. Ramps that do not meet the requirements shall be demolished and reconstructed during rectification. 1.2 At-Grade Crossing System 1.2.1 Crossing at At-Grade Intersections 1. Basic Principles A. The slow-traffic organization for pedestrians and non-motor vehicles within grade-separated interchange areas shall be continuous, safe, and convenient, and should be arranged at ground level to avoid pedestrians and non-motor vehicles having to go up and down or increasing detour distances. 2. Quality Enhancement A. Reducing crossing distance Reducing the curb radius at intersections can effectively lower turning speeds, shorten pedestrian crossing distances, and enlarge pedestrian waiting areas. The facility strip or green belt along the roadside may also be appropriately used to create a pedestrian stopping space. Table 1.2-1 Recommended Curb Radius Values | Road class | Recommended curb radius (m) | |---|---:| | Main and secondary arterial roads | 5–10 | | Branch roads | 5–8 | Note: For exclusive right-turn lanes with traffic islands, the recommended curb radius is 8–10 m. Figure 1.2-1 Reducing Road Curb Radius B. Secondary crossing refuge island When the pedestrian or bicycle crossing traverses more than 4 lanes of two-way motor vehicle traffic, or when the crossing length exceeds 16 m, a secondary crossing refuge island shall be set in the center of the road. The island width shall not be less than 2 m, and in difficult circumstances not less than 1.5 m. On roads with a median strip (or where lane width can be reduced), pedestrian crossings on signal-free sections shall be provided with a “Z”-shaped secondary crossing refuge island. The refuge island length shall not be less than 8 m, and corresponding guardrails shall be installed. Figure 1.2-2 Schematic Diagram of a “Z”-Shaped Secondary Crossing Refuge Island I C. All-direction cross intersection For intersections surrounded by relatively dense commercial facilities and heavy pedestrian flows, an “all-direction cross intersection” may be used as appropriate. This not only improves pedestrian crossing efficiency, but also prevents interference between pedestrians and motor vehicles. D. Improving the experience of non-motor vehicle crossings Intersections with large non-motor vehicle crossing volumes should be equipped with dedicated non-motor vehicle signal lights. At branch-road intersections with heavy non-motor vehicle traffic, explore moving the non-motor vehicle crossing waiting area in front of the motor vehicle stop line and granting an early green signal priority.
